title: How to Know Your Brake Pads Are Worn | Mechanix Pro
desc: Squeals, a soft lever and longer stopping are common signs of worn brake pads. Learn what to look and listen for, and why an inspection beats guessing.
h1: How to know your brake pads are worn
lead: Brake pads wear down slowly, so the change is easy to miss until stopping feels different. Here are the signs riders in Bengaluru can check for themselves.
sections: Listen for noise when you brake

A high squeal or a metal-on-metal grinding sound when you press the lever or pedal is one of the most common warnings. Some pads have a built-in wear indicator that makes noise on purpose once the lining gets thin.

Noise can also come from dust, moisture or a glazed surface, so a sound alone does not prove the pads are finished. It does mean the brakes deserve a proper look.

Try braking gently in a quiet spot and listen again. If the sound changes with speed or only appears when the brake is wet, mention that to your mechanic, since it helps narrow down the cause.
Feel how the brake responds

Worn pads often make the lever feel softer, or you may have to squeeze it further than before to get the same bite. Stopping distance can grow, which matters a lot in stop-and-go Bengaluru traffic.

A pulsing feel or a bike that pulls to one side when braking can point to uneven wear or a disc problem. Do not ignore either.

Front and rear brakes wear at different rates, and many riders lean on the front one more. Check both, and do not assume that one good brake means the other is fine.
What you can see

On many bikes you can look at the pad between the caliper and the disc. If the friction material looks very thin, close to the metal backing, it is time to replace it.

Drum brakes on some scooters and commuters hide the lining inside the drum, so you cannot check them by eye. A mechanic can open the drum and measure the lining properly.

Pads are not the only part. A disc with deep grooves, a ridge at the edge or a blue tint from heat also needs attention, and a mechanic can measure it against the limit your maker gives.
Why waiting costs more

Pads that wear all the way down can scratch the disc or damage the drum, which turns a small job into a bigger one. Brake fluid that is old or low can also change how the lever feels, so it is worth checking at the same time.

Brakes are a safety part. If you are unsure, get them inspected rather than guessing, and follow your owner's manual for the replacement guidance on your model.
Habits that make pads last longer

Look ahead and brake early and smoothly instead of grabbing the lever late. Hard, repeated stops in heavy traffic wear pads faster, and so does riding with the brake lightly dragging.

Keep the brakes clean. Mud and dust from a wet or dusty ride act like sandpaper between the pad and the disc. After a muddy ride, a gentle rinse and a dry-off helps.

Can I ride with worn brake pads?

title: Bike Chain Lubrication and Adjustment Basics | Mechanix Pro
desc: A dry or loose chain wears faster and wastes power. Learn how often to check it, how to clean and lube it, and how to judge slack on a commuter bike.
h1: Chain lubrication and adjustment for your bike
lead: The chain carries every bit of power to your rear wheel, yet it is often forgotten. A few minutes of care keeps it quiet and helps it last.
sections: Why the chain needs attention

A chain works in dust, grit and water. When it dries out or goes loose, it wears itself and the sprockets faster, and you may notice noise, jerks or a drop in smooth pickup.

Bengaluru's dust in summer and mud in the monsoon both pull oil away from the chain, so it needs checking more often than many riders expect.

A well-kept chain also makes the ride quieter and smoother. Many riders notice that once a noisy chain is cleaned and lubricated, the whole bike feels more relaxed.
Cleaning before you lubricate

Oiling a dirty chain just traps the grit. Wipe off old grease and mud with a rag, and use a chain cleaner or a soft brush if the dirt is thick. Avoid harsh solvents on chains with rubber seals, since they can damage the seals.

Let the chain dry for a short while before applying new lubricant.
How to lubricate it

Use a lubricant made for motorcycle chains. Apply a little to the inside run of the chain while turning the wheel slowly, then wipe off the extra so it does not fling onto the tyre or brake.

Keep lubricant away from the rear tyre and brake disc or drum at all times.

A good habit is to lubricate after the ride, not before, so the oil has time to settle into the links overnight. This keeps less of it flying off at speed.
Checking the slack

Your owner's manual gives the correct amount of chain play for your model. Check it with the bike on its stand, at the tightest point of the chain, because chains do not wear evenly.

A chain that is too tight strains the gearbox output and wheel bearings. One that is too loose can slip or jump off. If the chain is stretched, stiff in places or the sprockets look hooked, it is usually time to replace the set together.

Take a look at the rear sprocket teeth as well. Teeth that look sharp, hooked or uneven suggest the sprocket is worn, and a new chain on a worn sprocket will wear out quickly.
Chain types and sealed chains

Many bikes use an O-ring or X-ring chain, which has small rubber seals that keep grease inside. These last longer, but they still need cleaning and the right lubricant, and harsh cleaners can harm the seals.

Scooters often use a belt or a sealed chain case instead. If your scooter has a chain case, it may need oil or grease at intervals given in the manual, and a mechanic can check that.

faq: How often should I lubricate my bike chain?

Many riders do it every couple of weeks, and again after riding in rain or heavy dust. Your owner's manual may suggest a different interval, so follow that. A dry, noisy or rusty-looking chain needs attention sooner.
How do I know if my bike chain is too loose?

If the chain sags more than the play stated in your owner's manual, slaps against the swingarm, or makes jerks when you accelerate, it is likely too loose. Measure on the stand at the tightest point, or ask a mechanic.
Can I use engine oil on my chain?
It is not recommended. Engine oil flings off quickly and does not cling like chain lubricant. Use a lubricant made for motorcycle chains, and wipe off any extra so it stays off the tyre and brakes.

title: Engine Oil Change Interval Basics for Riders | Mechanix Pro
desc: Engine oil protects your engine, but the right interval depends on your bike. Learn the basics of oil changes, oil grades and signs it is overdue.
h1: Engine oil change: interval basics for riders
lead: Fresh oil is the cheapest protection your engine gets. The right interval depends on your bike, so here is how to work it out.
sections: What engine oil does

Oil lubricates moving parts, carries heat away and holds tiny particles in suspension so they do not scratch the engine. Over time it breaks down and gets loaded with dirt, and it stops doing these jobs well.

In many bikes it also lubricates the clutch and gearbox, so old oil can show up as clutch or gear trouble.

Oil does not only wear out by distance. Even a bike that is ridden very little can have oil that ages with time, which is why many manuals give a time limit as well as a distance.
Finding your interval

Your owner's manual or service booklet lists the oil change interval, usually by distance or time, whichever comes first. Many commuter bikes ask for a change every few thousand kilometres or every few months.

If you ride short trips in heavy traffic, the engine seldom gets fully warm and oil can age faster than the kilometre count suggests.

A good way to remember is to write the date and odometer reading on a small sticker or in your phone after each change. That way you always know when the next one is due.
Using the right oil

Use the grade and specification given in the manual. Thicker is not better, and mixing random oils can affect the clutch and fuel economy. Bikes and scooters can need different oils, so do not assume one fits all.

Synthetic, semi-synthetic and mineral oils all exist. Choose the type your maker allows, and ask your mechanic what is going in.
Signs oil is overdue

• Oil on the dipstick or sight glass looks very dark or gritty
  • The level is low between changes
  • The engine sounds rougher or hotter than usual
  • Gear changes feel notchy

A leak under the bike or smoke from the exhaust is not an interval issue. Get it inspected.
Checking the level yourself

Many bikes have a dipstick or a small window on the engine. Check the level with the bike upright on level ground, and follow the manual on whether the engine should be warm or cold for the reading.

Do not overfill. Too much oil can cause frothing, leaks and a rough-running engine. If the level drops often between changes, mention it to your mechanic, because it can point to a leak or burning oil.

faq: How often should I change engine oil in my bike?

Follow the interval in your owner's manual, usually by kilometres or months, whichever comes first. Many commuter bikes ask for a change every few thousand kilometres. Heavy city traffic can age oil faster, so change it sooner if it looks dark or low.
Does a scooter need the same oil as a bike?

Not always. Scooters and bikes can need different grades and specifications, especially where the clutch shares oil with the engine. Use exactly what your owner's manual specifies, and ask your mechanic to confirm before pouring.
What happens if I never change engine oil?

Old oil loses its ability to lubricate and cool, so parts wear faster and the engine can run hotter and rougher. Over time this can lead to expensive damage. Regular oil changes are one of the simplest ways to protect your engine.

title: Monsoon Bike Care in Bengaluru | Mechanix Pro
desc: Rain, waterlogged roads and mud are hard on bikes. A simple monsoon checklist for Bengaluru riders: brakes, tyres, chain, lights, battery and electricals.
h1: Monsoon bike care in Bengaluru
lead: Bengaluru rain turns roads slick and fills potholes you cannot see. A little preparation before the heavy showers saves a lot of trouble later.
sections: Brakes and tyres come first

Wet roads need good brakes and good grip. Have the pads, discs or drums checked, and look at the tyre tread and pressure. Smooth, worn tyres lose grip quickly on wet tarmac.

If anything feels soft or uneven, get it inspected before the rains peak.

Wet leaves, oil patches and painted road markings are especially slippery in the rain. Allow more distance to stop, and be gentle with both brakes together.
Protect the chain and electricals

Water washes lubricant off the chain, so clean and lube it more often during the monsoon. Rust can set in quickly if a wet chain is left alone.

Check the battery terminals, wiring joints, horn and lights for loose or corroded connections. Water in a connector can cause misfires or a bike that will not start.

A light spray of a water-displacing product on exposed electrical connectors can help, as long as it is made for that use. Keep it off brakes and tyres.
Riding through standing water

Avoid deep water if you can. If the engine takes in water through the air intake or exhaust, it can stall and may suffer serious damage. Do not try to restart a bike that died in water. Push it to a dry spot and call for help.

Ride slowly and steadily, and test your brakes lightly after crossing water to dry them.
After the ride

Rinse off mud, but keep high-pressure water away from bearings, electrical parts and the air box. Dry the bike with a cloth, and dry the chain before lubricating.

Parking under cover helps. If you must park outside, a good cover that breathes is better than plastic that traps moisture.

Check the seat and storage areas on scooters. Water can collect under the seat, and wet items left there can cause damp and rust.
Visibility and riding in rain

Rain cuts visibility for you and for others. Make sure your headlight, tail light and brake light work, keep the visor or helmet clean, and wear bright or reflective gear when you can.

Leave extra space from the vehicle ahead. Brake earlier and smoother than usual, and avoid sudden turns, especially on painted lines, manhole covers and metal plates.

faq: How do I protect my bike during the monsoon?

Check brakes and tyres, keep the chain clean and lubricated, inspect the battery, wiring and lights, and park under cover when you can. A pre-monsoon service helps catch small issues before wet roads make them worse.
What should I do if my bike stalls in water?
Do not keep trying to start it. Water can enter the engine and cause serious damage. Push the bike to a dry safe spot, switch it off and call for roadside help so a mechanic can check it first.
Is it bad to wash my bike with a pressure washer in the rain season?

High pressure can push water into bearings, electrical connectors and the air box. Use gentle water flow, keep spray away from those parts, and dry the bike and chain afterwards to prevent rust. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

title: Puncture: Tube vs Tubeless and Roadside Tips | Mechanix Pro
desc: Tube and tubeless tyres fail differently. Learn the difference, what to do when you get a puncture on the road, and when a repair is not safe.
h1: Puncture: tube vs tubeless and what to do on the road
lead: A puncture can happen to any rider. Knowing what kind of tyre you have, and what to do next, keeps a bad moment from getting worse.
sections: Tube tyres and tubeless tyres

A tube-type tyre has an inner tube that holds the air. When it is punctured, air usually escapes fast and the tyre goes flat quickly. A tubeless tyre holds air directly against the rim and often loses air more slowly when a small object is stuck in it.

Your tyre sidewall and owner's manual tell you which type your bike uses. Do not assume.

Some bikes with spoked wheels use tube-type tyres, while many bikes with alloy wheels use tubeless tyres. This is a general pattern, not a rule, so check your own bike.
Signs of a puncture

• The bike feels heavy or wobbly at the rear or front
  • Steering feels vague
  • You hear a flapping sound
  • One tyre looks lower than the other

Slow down gently. Do not brake hard or turn sharply.

Check your tyres by eye before every ride. Many punctures are found early by a quick look at the tread and a press of the tyre with your thumb.
What to do on the road

Pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic, and switch on your hazard lights if you have them. Do not ride far on a flat tyre, because it can damage the rim and the tyre itself and make steering unsafe.

If a nail or object is stuck in a tubeless tyre, leave it in place. It may be sealing the hole. Call for help rather than pulling it out.
Repair or replace

Small punctures in the tread area can often be repaired. Sidewall damage, large cuts, bulges or a tyre that has been ridden flat should not be repaired and need a professional opinion.

Tyres are a safety part, so have the repair checked by a mechanic.

Do not use quick-fix sprays or sealants without asking a mechanic. They can hide a problem and may not suit your tyre type.
Carrying the right basics

A small portable inflator can help with a slow leak. If your bike has tubeless tyres, a basic plug kit is something some riders carry, though it is only a temporary fix and the tyre should be properly inspected soon after.

Whatever you carry, know how to use it before you need it. If you are not confident, it is safer to call for help than to attempt a roadside repair in traffic.

faq: What is the difference between tube and tubeless tyres?

A tube tyre uses an inner tube to hold air, so a puncture usually deflates it quickly. A tubeless tyre seals air against the rim, so small punctures often leak slowly. Check your owner's manual to know which type your bike has.
Should I remove the nail from my tubeless tyre?
No. Leave it in. It may be plugging the hole and slowing the air loss. Ride no further than necessary, or better still, stop and call for help so the tyre can be checked and repaired properly.
Can I ride a bike with a flat tyre to a repair shop?
Avoid it. Riding on a flat tyre can damage the tyre and rim, and makes steering unsafe. It is better to stop somewhere safe and get help to come to you or arrange a pickup.

title: Bike Not Starting? Battery and Starter Checks | Mechanix Pro
desc: If your bike will not self-start, the battery may not be the only cause. Simple checks for kick and self-start, and when to call a mechanic.
h1: Bike won't start: battery and self-start checks
lead: A bike that clicks but does not start is frustrating, especially on a weekday morning. These simple checks help you narrow down the cause.
sections: Start with the obvious

Make sure the kill switch is in the run position, the side stand is up if your bike has a stand cut-off, the gear is in neutral or the clutch is pulled, and there is fuel in the tank. These simple things cause more no-starts than people expect.

Then check that the ignition is on and the dashboard lights up.

Keep the side stand in mind. Many bikes have a safety switch that stops the engine from starting, or cuts it, when the stand is down.
Reading the battery signs

Dim lights, a weak horn or a slow, clicking self-start usually point to a low battery. A battery that is old, deeply discharged or left unused for weeks can fail to turn the engine over.

Loose or corroded battery terminals can also cut power. Do not poke around electrical parts if you are unsure.

A battery can look fine and still be weak. The only reliable way to know is to test it with a meter or a load tester, which a mechanic can do in a few minutes.
Try the kick start

If your bike has a kick starter, it is a useful test. If it starts on the kick but not the self-start, the battery or starter circuit is the likely suspect. If it will not start either way, look at fuel, spark and air.

Many modern bikes have no kick start, so do not force a method your bike does not have.
When the battery is not the problem

A faulty starter relay, a failing spark plug, a blocked fuel line or a dirty air filter can all mimic a weak battery. Repeated cranking can drain the battery further, so give it short attempts with pauses.

Do not jump-start a bike from a car engine that is running. Voltage spikes can damage the electronics.

A bike that starts fine when cold but not when hot, or the other way around, gives your mechanic a useful clue, so note when the problem happens.
Looking after the battery

Short trips and long idling do not give the battery much time to recharge. If you mostly ride short distances, a longer ride now and then helps keep the battery topped up.

Avoid leaving the ignition on with the engine off, and avoid adding extra electrical accessories without checking the load. Keep the terminals clean, dry and tight.

faq: Why does my bike click but not start?

A clicking sound with no start often means the battery is too weak to turn the starter, or the terminals are loose or corroded. A faulty starter relay can also cause it. A mechanic can test the battery and charging system.
How long does a bike battery last?

It depends on the battery, your riding and how often the bike is used. Batteries wear out over time and fail sooner if the bike sits unused. If starting becomes slow, have the battery and charging system tested.
Can I start my bike with a kick if the battery is dead?

If your bike has a kick starter, usually yes, though the lights and indicators may stay weak. Many modern bikes have no kick starter. If yours does not, you will need a battery charge, replacement or a mechanic's help.

title: Clutch Slipping or Heavy Lever: Common Causes | Mechanix Pro
desc: A slipping clutch or a stiff lever is rarely something to ignore. Learn the common causes, simple checks and when to book a mechanic.
h1: Clutch problems: slipping and a heavy lever
lead: The clutch takes a beating in Bengaluru's stop-start traffic. Two problems show up most: slipping and a lever that feels heavy.
sections: What a slipping clutch feels like

The engine revs rise but the bike does not speed up as it should, especially going uphill or when you pull away with a pillion. You may also notice a burning smell.

Slipping wears the clutch plates fast, so do not keep riding in this state.

A clutch that drags is the opposite problem, where the bike creeps forward or the gears crunch when you try to change. It also needs adjusting or inspection.
Common causes of slipping

• Worn friction plates from heavy use
  • No free play in the clutch cable, so the clutch never fully engages
  • Old or wrong engine oil, which can affect wet clutches
  • Weak clutch springs

Riding with the clutch half pulled in traffic speeds up wear, so try to avoid it.

Heavy loads and frequent pillion riding add strain, so a bike that carries two people daily may need clutch attention earlier than one that is ridden solo.
Why the lever feels heavy

A dry, rusty or frayed cable is a common reason. The lever pivot can also be dry or dirty. A cable routed with sharp bends adds drag too.

Lubricating the cable and the lever pivot often helps. A cable that is badly worn should be replaced.
Checks you can do

Look at the free play at the lever end and compare it with your owner's manual. Check that the cable moves smoothly and is not frayed. If the lever feels hard or the clutch drags in gear at a standstill, it needs adjusting.

Do not over-tighten the cable. Too little free play can cause slipping.

A hydraulic clutch has no cable, but the fluid level and condition still matter. If the lever feels spongy or does not return properly, have it checked.
Riding habits that protect the clutch

Pull the lever fully and release it smoothly, rather than slipping the clutch to creep forward in traffic. Use the right gear for the speed, and avoid pulling away in a high gear.

Shift to neutral at long waits and avoid resting your fingers on the lever while riding. Small habits like these add up over months of Bengaluru traffic.

faq: Why is my bike clutch slipping?

Common reasons are worn clutch plates, a cable with no free play, old or incorrect engine oil, or weak springs. Revs rising without matching speed is the typical sign. Avoid hard riding and have a mechanic inspect it soon.
Why is my clutch lever so heavy?

Often it is a dry, rusty or frayed cable, or a dry lever pivot. Lubricating them can help. If the lever remains stiff, the cable may need replacing or the clutch mechanism may need a proper inspection.
Is it okay to ride with a half-pulled clutch in traffic?

It is best avoided. Holding the clutch partly pulled makes the plates slip and wear faster. Use neutral when you are stopped for a while, and release the lever fully when you are moving. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

title: Air Filter: Why It Matters for Mileage | Mechanix Pro
desc: A clogged air filter can make your bike run rich and drink more fuel. Learn what it does, how to spot a dirty one and why Bengaluru dust matters.
h1: Air filter: why it matters for your bike's mileage
lead: Your engine needs clean air to burn fuel properly. A choked filter is a quiet cause of poor mileage and weak pickup.
sections: What the air filter does

Every engine mixes air with fuel. The filter stops dust and grit from entering the engine, where they would scratch the cylinder and piston.

When the filter clogs, less air gets in, and the mix can turn too rich. That wastes fuel.

A clean filter also protects the engine over the long run. Dust that gets past a damaged filter acts like fine sandpaper inside the cylinder.
Signs of a dirty filter

• Mileage that has dropped without another clear reason
  • Sluggish pickup or a bike that feels choked
  • Black smoke from the exhaust
  • Rough idle or harder starting

These can also come from other faults, so a check is better than guessing.

Take a look at the filter housing when you service the bike. Cracks, loose clips or a poorly seated element let dirty air bypass the filter altogether.
Dust makes a difference

Bengaluru's roadwork and construction dust can load a filter faster than you expect. Riders who often use unpaved roads or heavy traffic corridors may need to check it more often than the manual's minimum.

Some bikes use a paper element, others a foam one. Paper is usually replaced, foam may be cleaned and re-oiled if the maker allows it.
What not to do

Do not blow compressed air hard through a paper filter, or wash it with water, unless the manual says so. You can damage the element.

Running without a filter is never a good idea.

Do not soak a paper filter in oil. Oil is for foam filters only, and only when the manual says so. Too much oil on a foam filter can also choke the engine.
How often to look

A quick look at each service is a good habit. If you ride through dusty roadwork often, ask your mechanic to look at it in between. It takes a few minutes and costs little compared with the fuel a clogged filter can waste.

After riding in heavy rain or through water, check that the air box has not taken in moisture, as a wet filter can cause rough running or stalling.

faq: Does a dirty air filter reduce mileage?

It can. A clogged filter restricts airflow, so the engine may burn a richer mix and use more fuel. Pickup can also feel weaker. Other faults cause similar symptoms, so a mechanic's check is the best way to be sure.
How often should I change my bike's air filter?

Follow your owner's manual, which gives an interval or inspection schedule. If you ride in a lot of dust or on unpaved roads, check it more often. A visibly dirty or oily filter should be cleaned or replaced.
Can I clean a paper air filter myself?

Usually not. Paper elements are generally replaced rather than cleaned, and washing or blasting them with air can damage them. Foam filters can sometimes be cleaned if your manual allows it. Ask a mechanic if unsure.

title: Spark Plug Basics for Bike and Scooter Riders | Mechanix Pro
desc: A worn spark plug can cause hard starting, rough running and poor mileage. Learn what it does, how to read its condition and when to replace it.
h1: Spark plug basics for riders
lead: The spark plug is a small part with a big job. Here is what it does and how to tell when it needs attention.
sections: What a spark plug does

It creates the spark that ignites the fuel and air mix in the cylinder. If the spark is weak or late, the fuel burns poorly, and the engine runs rough.

Plugs wear over time because the gap between the electrodes slowly grows.

Some bikes have more than one plug per cylinder, and some use long-life plugs. Your manual tells you what applies to your model.
Signs of a tired plug

• Hard starting, especially when cold
  • Misfiring or hesitation when you open the throttle
  • A rough or unsteady idle
  • Poor mileage or weak pickup

Other faults can look the same, so a check is wiser than guessing.

A plug that has been misfiring for a while can also wash fuel into the engine oil, which is another reason not to ignore a rough-running bike.
What the plug can tell you

A mechanic can read the colour and deposits on the plug tip. A light tan or greyish-brown tip is usually considered healthy. Black, sooty deposits can hint at a rich mix. Oily deposits can point to oil getting into the cylinder. A white, blistered tip can suggest overheating.

These are clues, not a diagnosis, so the cause still needs to be checked.
Use the right plug

Use the plug type and gap that your owner's manual lists. A wrong heat range or a loosely fitted plug can cause damage. Over-tightening can damage the threads in the cylinder head.

Replace plugs at the interval in your manual, or earlier if they look worn.

Never test a plug by touching it while the engine is running. The ignition system carries a high voltage that can give a nasty shock.
Why plugs foul

Short trips, long idling and a rich fuel mix are common reasons for a fouled plug in city riding. A weak battery, a dirty air filter or the wrong oil can also play a part.

If a new plug fouls quickly, the plug is probably not the root cause. Ask your mechanic to look at the air filter, the fuel mix and the engine condition, instead of just changing plugs again and again.

faq: When should I replace my bike's spark plug?

Follow the interval in your owner's manual. Replace it sooner if the bike starts hard, misfires or loses mileage and the plug looks worn, sooty or oily. A mechanic can inspect it and advise whether cleaning or replacing makes sense.
Can a bad spark plug reduce mileage?
Yes. A weak or fouled plug can cause incomplete burning, so the engine wastes fuel and loses pickup. Other issues can cause the same symptoms, so have the plug and other basics checked by a mechanic.
What does a black spark plug mean?

Black sooty deposits often suggest a rich fuel mix, a dirty air filter or short, slow trips. It is a clue, not a final diagnosis. A mechanic can check the air filter, carburettor or injector and correct the cause.

title: Coolant and Overheating in Bengaluru Traffic | Mechanix Pro
desc: Liquid-cooled bikes and scooters can overheat in slow traffic. Learn how coolant works, the warning signs and what to do if the temperature climbs.
h1: Coolant and overheating in slow traffic
lead: Long waits at signals and crawling traffic do not give your engine much airflow. Coolant and the cooling fan have to do the work.
sections: Which bikes use coolant

Many newer bikes and some scooters are liquid-cooled. Others are air-cooled or oil-cooled. Your owner's manual says which you have, and what coolant to use.

If your bike is liquid-cooled, the coolant level and condition matter all year, not only in summer.

Air-cooled engines rely on airflow and their fins to lose heat, so they can also run hot in slow traffic, even though they have no coolant to check.
Warning signs of overheating

• The temperature gauge or warning light climbs
  • The engine loses power or pings
  • You smell hot coolant or see steam
  • The cooling fan runs constantly or not at all

Pull over safely if you see any of these.

If the fan never seems to come on in traffic, or runs and the temperature still climbs, mention both to your mechanic. These are useful clues.
What to do if it overheats

Switch off the engine in a safe spot and let it cool. Never open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot, because hot coolant can spray out under pressure.

Do not pour cold water onto a hot engine. Once it is cool, check for leaks and the coolant level, and call for help if you are not sure.
Keeping the cooling system healthy

Check the level in the reservoir against the marks, when the engine is cold. Coolant ages, so follow the replacement guidance in your manual. Keep the radiator fins clear of mud and dust, and look at hoses for cracks or seepage.

Use the coolant type your maker specifies. Mixing types can cause problems.

Using plain water for long periods is not ideal, because coolant also protects against corrosion and boiling. Follow the maker's guidance on the mix.
Riding tips for hot days

Avoid revving hard while stuck in traffic, and switch off the engine at long waits if it is safe to do so. A bike that sits and idles in the sun gets hot quickly.

If you are on a long trip, take breaks and check the gauge now and then. Keep a close eye on the engine temperature if you are carrying a pillion or a heavy load.

faq: Why does my bike overheat in traffic?

In slow traffic there is little airflow over the engine, so the cooling system works harder. Low coolant, a weak fan, a blocked radiator or old coolant can make it worse. A mechanic can check the cooling system.
Can I open the radiator cap when the engine is hot?
No. Hot coolant is under pressure and can spray out and cause burns. Switch off the engine, wait until it is fully cool, and then check the level. If you are unsure, ask a mechanic to do it.
How often should I change bike coolant?
Follow your owner's manual, which gives a time or distance interval and the type of coolant to use. Coolant ages even if the bike is not used much, so a periodic check is a good habit.

title: Scooter CVT Belt and Rollers: The Basics | Mechanix Pro
desc: Most automatic scooters use a CVT with a belt and rollers. Learn what they do, the signs of wear and why they matter for smooth, steady pickup.
h1: Scooter CVT belt and rollers: the basics
lead: If you ride an automatic scooter, a belt and a set of rollers decide how smoothly it pulls away. They wear quietly, so it helps to know the signs.
sections: What the CVT does

A CVT, or continuously variable transmission, replaces gears with a belt that runs between two pulleys. The rollers inside the front pulley move outward as the engine speeds up, changing the drive ratio smoothly.

Because there is no gear lever, the scooter feels simple to ride, but the parts still wear with use.

Some scooters have a small drive belt cover with an air intake. Keeping that intake clear stops dust from building up in the case and wearing the belt faster.
Signs of a worn belt

• Jerky or hesitant pickup
  • A slipping feel, with revs rising more than speed
  • A squeal or slapping noise from the transmission area
  • Weaker top speed than before

A belt that is cracked, frayed or glazed is near the end of its life.

A belt that has been run hot or overloaded can look fine but still lose its grip, so symptoms often matter more than looks.
Rollers and the front pulley

Rollers can flatten or wear unevenly, which causes vibration at certain speeds and delayed acceleration. Worn rollers also change how the scooter feels when pulling away with a pillion.

The pulley faces and the clutch bell can wear too. They are usually checked together.
Care that helps

Follow the manual for belt and roller inspection intervals. Keep the CVT cover and air duct clean, because dust and water inside accelerate wear. After heavy rain or flooding, have the CVT area checked.

Do not use oil or grease on the belt or pulleys. It makes the belt slip.

Heavy loads, steep hills and frequent stop-start riding all strain the CVT, which is common for scooter riders in the city.
Other parts worth checking

The clutch shoes and the clutch bell are part of the same system. Worn shoes cause a delayed or shuddering pull-away, and a scored bell can make the scooter vibrate.

The slider pieces and the pulley springs can also wear. A mechanic usually checks all of these together when the CVT cover is opened, which saves you from paying for labour twice.

Your owner's manual gives an inspection or replacement schedule, which varies by model. Heavy city riding, carrying a pillion often and water exposure can wear a belt faster, so watch for symptoms between services. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Can I put grease on a scooter belt to stop the noise?
No. Oil or grease on the belt or pulleys makes the belt slip and wear faster. If the transmission is noisy, have the CVT area inspected and cleaned by a mechanic instead of adding lubricant.

title: Electric Scooter Care in Bengaluru | Mechanix Pro
desc: Electric scooters have no engine oil, but still need care. A practical guide to battery habits, charging, tyres, brakes and checks for Bengaluru riders.
h1: Electric scooter care in Bengaluru
lead: An electric scooter has fewer moving parts than a petrol one, but it is not maintenance-free. Good habits help the battery and the rest of the bike last.
sections: Battery and charging habits

Follow the charging advice from your scooter's maker. In general, avoid leaving the battery fully drained for long periods, and avoid charging in direct sun or a very hot, closed space.

Use the charger that came with the scooter, or one the maker approves. A cheap, mismatched charger can harm the battery.

Plan your charging around your routine. Topping up a little often is usually fine, but the maker's advice for your battery type always comes first.
Brakes, tyres and suspension

Electric scooters are heavy because of the battery, so brakes and tyres work hard. Check tyre pressure often and look at brake pads or shoes for wear. Regenerative braking on some models does not replace working mechanical brakes.

Potholes can stress the suspension, so listen for knocks and look for oil leaks.

Keep the tyres at the pressure given by the maker, since the weight of the battery and the rider makes correct pressure even more important.
Water and electrics

Most electric scooters are built to handle rain, but standing water, high-pressure washing and flooded roads can still cause problems. Keep water away from the charging port and connectors, and dry them if they get wet.

If a warning light stays on or the range suddenly drops, get it checked.
Signs to watch for

• Range that falls noticeably over time
  • Charging that stops early or takes longer than usual
  • Unusual heat, smell or swelling around the battery area
  • Warning lights or jerky power delivery

Do not open the battery pack yourself.

Software updates and fault codes are handled by the maker or an authorised service point. We tell you honestly when a problem falls into that group.
Everyday habits that help

Park in shade or under cover when you can, because heat is hard on batteries. Avoid riding through deep puddles, and wipe the scooter dry after a wet ride.

Do a quick walk-around now and then. Look at the tyres, brakes, lights and the condition of cables and connectors. Small problems found early tend to be cheaper and simpler to fix.

faq: Do electric scooters need servicing?

Yes. There is no engine oil to change, but brakes, tyres, suspension, lights, connectors and battery health still need regular checks. If the range drops or charging behaves oddly, get the scooter inspected. Ask for an itemised quote on WhatsApp before any work starts.
How can I make my electric scooter battery last longer?

Use the charger your maker supplies, avoid charging in extreme heat, avoid leaving the battery fully drained for long periods and follow the manual. Regular checks catch problems early. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Can I ride an electric scooter in heavy Bengaluru rain?

Most are built to handle normal rain, but avoid deep standing water and high-pressure washing near connectors and the charging port. Check your owner's manual for the maker's guidance, and have it inspected after any flooding.

title: How to Read a Bike Service Quote | Mechanix Pro
desc: A good quote lists every part and labour item clearly. Learn how to read a bike service quote, ask the right questions and spot padding before you pay.
h1: How to read a bike service quote and spot padding
lead: A service quote should be easy to understand. If it is vague, rushed or full of extras you did not ask for, slow down and ask questions.
sections: What a clear quote looks like

It lists each job and each part as a separate line, with the labour shown clearly. You should be able to see what is being done and why, without needing to decode abbreviations.

A vague line like "general work" or "miscellaneous" is a reason to ask for more detail.

Check that your bike's name and registration are correct on the quote. It sounds simple, but it avoids mix-ups about which parts and which model were quoted.
Questions worth asking

• Which parts will be replaced, and which are only being cleaned or adjusted?
  • Are the parts OEM or aftermarket?
  • Is this part worn out now, or only due later?
  • Can I keep the old part?

A good mechanic answers these without fuss.

Ask whether the labour is a fixed amount for the job or charged by time. Knowing this up front helps you compare quotes between providers.
Common signs of padding

Be careful with a long list of replacements on a bike that rides well, parts replaced when only cleaning was needed, or pressure to approve everything on the spot. Another warning sign is a quote that changes during the work without asking you.

Not every extra is padding. Some parts really are worn. The difference is that an honest quote explains the reason.
Urgent vs can wait

Ask the mechanic to split items into safety-critical, soon and can wait. Brakes, tyres and steering are things you should not delay. A cosmetic or minor item can often wait for the next service.

You are free to say no to anything you do not understand.

If a mechanic says a part must be replaced, ask to see the old part and what is wrong with it. A fair mechanic is happy to show you.
Compare before you decide

If a quote feels high or confusing, ask another provider for the same list of work, and compare the lines side by side. Do not compare only the total, because different parts and different jobs can make the totals look similar or very different.

Make sure you are comparing like with like: the same parts quality, the same scope and the same warranty. A cheaper quote that leaves things out is not really cheaper.

faq: How do I know if a mechanic is padding the bill?

Warning signs are vague quote lines, many replacements on a bike that rides well, pressure to approve on the spot and changes to the quote mid-job. Ask what is worn and why, and ask for an itemised quote.
Should I ask for a written quote before service?

Yes. A written, itemised quote shows each part and labour line, so you can compare, ask questions and approve only what you want. It also avoids surprises when you get the final bill. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.

title: OEM vs Aftermarket Bike Parts Explained | Mechanix Pro
desc: OEM and aftermarket parts both have a place. Learn the difference, what to ask your mechanic and when each choice makes sense for your bike.
h1: OEM vs aftermarket parts, explained simply
lead: You will hear both terms when you get a quote. Neither is automatically good or bad. What matters is quality, fit and being told what you are getting.
sections: What OEM means

OEM stands for original equipment manufacturer. An OEM part is made to the same specification as the part your bike came with, and usually comes through the maker's own channel.

It is the safe choice for fit and expected performance, and often the one linked to the maker's warranty.

OEM parts usually come in the maker's box, with batch or part numbers. If a part comes with no packaging or marking, ask where it comes from.
What aftermarket means

Aftermarket parts are made by other companies. Quality varies widely, from very good to poor. Some are made by the same suppliers that make OEM parts. Others are cheap copies.

Aftermarket parts can offer more choice, and sometimes better value, when they come from a trusted brand.

A trusted aftermarket brand usually has a track record and a warranty. A brand nobody can name usually has neither.
When OEM is the better pick

For safety-critical parts such as brake pads, and for anything where exact fit matters, many riders prefer OEM. If your bike is new and under the maker's warranty, check the warranty terms before using other parts.

Your owner's manual and service booklet explain what the maker expects.
When aftermarket can make sense

For consumables on an older bike, a good aftermarket brand can be a sensible option. The key is knowing the brand and not just the price.

Avoid unbranded parts with no box, no batch details and no seller you can ask.

Ask your mechanic to write the brand of each part on the quote. It lets you check the brand later and keep a record for future servicing.
Questions to ask about parts

Is this part OEM or aftermarket? Which brand is it? Does it carry a warranty of its own? Is it the exact part for my model and year?

A good mechanic answers these easily. If the answers are vague, that is a signal to slow down and ask for more detail before you agree.
What we do

faq: What is the difference between OEM and aftermarket parts?

OEM parts match the specification of the parts your bike was built with. Aftermarket parts come from other makers and vary in quality. Both can be good if they are from a trusted source and fit properly.
Are aftermarket parts safe to use on a bike?

Good aftermarket parts from trusted brands can be fine, but quality varies. For safety parts like brake pads, ask your mechanic which brand is being used, and consider OEM if you are unsure. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Will aftermarket parts void my bike warranty?

It depends on the maker's terms. Check your warranty booklet or ask the dealer before using non-OEM parts on a new bike. Using the wrong parts can affect a claim, so confirm first. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

A standard service adds items like air filter, spark plug and cable checks to the basics. A full service goes deeper, including suspension, fuel system and bearings, and is suited to bikes overdue for care.

desc: Heading out of Bengaluru for a long ride? Check tyres, brakes, chain, oil, lights and battery first. A simple checklist to ride with confidence.
h1: How to prepare your bike for a long ride
lead: A long ride tests every part of your bike for hours at a time. A proper check beforehand is cheaper and calmer than fixing a problem far from home.
sections: Start with tyres and brakes

Check tyre pressure when the tyres are cold, and set it as your owner's manual advises for the load you will carry. Look for cuts, bulges, embedded objects and low tread. Test the brakes and check pad thickness and fluid level.

If anything looks doubtful, get it inspected before you leave.

Do a short test ride after any checks or repairs, so that any new noise or feel shows up before the real trip begins.
Oil, chain and fluids

Make sure the engine oil level is right and the oil is not overdue. Clean and lubricate the chain, and check the slack. Look at coolant on liquid-cooled bikes, and brake and clutch fluid where fitted.

A fresh service before a long trip is a sensible habit.

Check for oil seepage around the engine and the fork seals. A small leak at home can become a bigger one after hours at highway speed.
Lights, battery and controls

Check the headlight, tail light, brake light and indicators. Make sure the horn works. If the bike has been slow to start, have the battery tested before you go.

Check that the throttle returns smoothly, and that the clutch and brake levers feel normal.
Load and tools

Pack light and balance the load. Carry a basic tool kit, a puncture repair or inflation option if suited to your tyres, a torch, your documents and a power bank. Save the number of roadside help on your phone.

Plan fuel stops and breaks, because tired riders make mistakes.

Wear proper gear: a good helmet, gloves, a jacket and sturdy shoes. Good gear is part of preparing the rider as well as the bike.
On the day of the ride

Start with a walk-around: tyres, lights, chain, mirrors and fuel. Start early so you are not rushing, and keep a steady pace instead of pushing hard to make up time.

Stop every so often to stretch, drink water and look the bike over. Feel the wheels and the engine area for unusual heat, and listen for anything new.

faq: What should I check before a long bike ride?

Check tyre pressure and condition, brakes, oil level, chain, lights, battery and controls. Carry basic tools, documents and a charged phone. A service before the trip catches issues that are hard to fix on the road.
Should I service my bike before a long trip?

title: Potholes: Suspension and Fork Checks | Mechanix Pro
desc: Bengaluru potholes punish suspension. Learn the signs of worn shocks and fork seals, what to check and why a bent rim or loose parts matter.
h1: Riding in potholes: suspension and fork checks
lead: Potholes are part of riding in Bengaluru. Your suspension absorbs the hits, but it does not last forever.
sections: What suspension does

Front forks and rear shock absorbers keep the wheels in contact with the road and soak up bumps. When they wear, the bike feels harsh or floaty, and braking and cornering can feel less stable.

Good suspension is about control, not only comfort.

Tyre pressure plays a role here too. Tyres at the right pressure absorb part of every bump and protect the rim.
Signs something is wrong

• Oil on the fork tubes, which can mean a leaking seal
  • The bike bounces more than usual after a bump
  • Knocking or clunking over rough roads
  • The front dives sharply under braking
  • The handlebar feels off-centre or the bike pulls to one side

A pull or wobble after hitting a big pothole needs a check.

A bike that feels unstable at speed after hitting a pothole may have a bent wheel or a loose steering head, so it deserves a check before the next fast ride.
After a hard hit

Look at the wheel rim for dents, and spin the wheel to see if it runs true. Check tyre pressure, because a hard impact can pinch the tyre. Look for loose nuts, a bent handlebar or fork tubes that look out of line.

If the bike does not feel right, do not keep riding it hard.
Ways to reduce the damage

Slow down before a pothole rather than braking in it, and keep the bike upright. Keep tyre pressure right, because under-inflated tyres are more likely to pinch and damage the rim. Do not overload the bike.

Service intervals for fork oil are in your manual.

Rear shock preload can often be adjusted for load. Check your manual to see whether your bike allows it and what setting is advised for a pillion.
Other parts hit by bad roads

Potholes also loosen bolts, crack plastics and damage the exhaust, the stands and the number plate bracket. A quick look for anything loose or hanging after a rough stretch can save you from losing a part.

Wheel bearings and steering head bearings take impact loads too. If you hear a rumble that changes with speed, or the steering feels notchy, have them checked.
Suspension checks at home

Our certified mechanics check forks, shock absorbers, bearings and wheel condition at your doorstep in Bengaluru, and tell you if a job needs a workshop. You get a quote on WhatsApp first. See the service packages and prices.
faq: How do I know if my bike's fork seal is leaking?
Look for oil on the fork tube or around the seal, often with dust stuck to it. You may also feel a softer front end. A leaking fork seal needs inspection and repair, since oil can reach the brakes.
Can potholes damage a bike's suspension?
Yes. Repeated or hard hits wear shock absorbers and fork seals, and can bend rims or loosen parts. After a hard impact, check the wheel and tyre, and have the bike inspected if it feels different.
Why does my bike feel bouncy over bumps?

Worn rear shock absorbers or tired fork oil are common causes, as is incorrect tyre pressure or an overloaded bike. A mechanic can check the suspension and tell you what needs attention. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

title: Why Your Bike Stalls at Signals | Mechanix Pro
desc: A bike that cuts out at a red light is annoying and risky. Learn the common causes, from idle setting to fuel and air problems, and when to book a check.
h1: Why a bike stalls at signals
lead: Stalling in the middle of traffic is stressful. It usually comes down to idle, air, fuel or spark, and most causes are simple to fix once found.
sections: Idle speed too low

If the idle setting has drifted, the engine may not have enough speed to keep running when you release the throttle. This is common after cold starts or when the air filter is dirty.

A mechanic can reset the idle properly. Do not turn screws randomly.

A bike that stalls only when the headlight or indicators come on can be pointing to a weak battery or charging fault, which is a useful clue.
Air and fuel problems

A clogged air filter, a dirty carburettor jet or a fouled fuel injector can upset the mix, and the engine may die at idle. Old or poor-quality fuel, and water in the fuel, can do the same.

On fuel-injected bikes, a dirty throttle body can also cause stalling.

On carburetted bikes, the pilot jet is a tiny passage that controls idle. It blocks easily, and cleaning it often fixes stalling.
Spark and electrical causes

A worn spark plug, a weak coil or loose electrical connections can cause the engine to misfire and cut out. A tired battery or a weak charging system can also upset the ignition on some bikes.

If the stalling comes with warning lights, get the bike scanned.
Other things to check

A cold engine that stalls but runs fine once warm can point to the choke or cold-start system. Heat can also make an engine stall in slow traffic, so check the cooling system on liquid-cooled bikes.

Look for any fuel smell or leaks.

Note whether the stall happens when the engine is cold, hot or both, and whether it restarts easily. These clues help your mechanic find the cause faster.
What to do while stopped

If your bike has a habit of stalling, hold the throttle very slightly open at signals, and avoid releasing the clutch suddenly when pulling away. This is only a short-term workaround.

Do not keep riding for weeks with the problem. A bike that cuts out in the middle of a junction puts you at risk, and the fault may also be harming the engine.

faq: Why does my bike switch off at a red light?

Common causes include low idle speed, a dirty air filter or carburettor, fuel problems, a worn spark plug or weak electrics. A mechanic can check each of these and set the idle correctly. Ask for an itemised quote on WhatsApp before any work starts.
Can bad petrol make a bike stall?

Yes. Poor quality fuel, or fuel with water in it, can cause rough running and stalling. If the problem began right after refuelling, tell your mechanic. The tank and fuel system may need cleaning. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Should I keep riding if my bike stalls often?

It is better not to. Frequent stalling in traffic is a safety risk, and the cause can get worse. Have the bike checked soon, and avoid busy roads until it is fixed. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

title: Mileage Drop: 7 Common Causes | Mechanix Pro
desc: Is your bike giving fewer kilometres per litre? Seven common causes, from tyre pressure to a dirty air filter, and how to find out which one it is.
h1: Mileage drop: seven common causes
lead: When mileage falls, the cause is often something small and fixable. Work through these seven before assuming the worst.
sections: 1 and 2: Tyres and chain

Low tyre pressure increases rolling resistance, so the engine works harder. A dry, loose or badly adjusted chain wastes power too. Both are quick to check.

Set pressure as your manual says, and clean and lubricate the chain regularly.

Check the pressure of both tyres, not just one, and use a proper gauge instead of pressing with your thumb.
3 and 4: Air filter and spark plug

A clogged air filter restricts airflow and can make the mix too rich. A worn spark plug leads to incomplete burning. Either one can cost you fuel and pickup.

Both are routine service items, so check them at each service.

A worn chain and sprocket set takes more effort to turn, so replacing them together is usually the better approach.
5 and 6: Old oil and dragging brakes

Old or wrong-grade engine oil increases friction inside the engine. Brakes that drag, because of a sticking caliper or an over-tight adjustment, make the bike work against itself.

If one wheel feels hot after a short ride, get the brake checked.

Heavy traffic and a stop-start rhythm use more fuel than steady riding, and no repair can change that, so judge mileage against your own past figures.
7: Riding style and load

Harsh acceleration, high speeds, long idling and frequent clutch riding use more fuel. So does carrying extra weight. Stop-start Bengaluru traffic makes all of this harder.

Smooth throttle use, early gear changes and switching off at long waits can help.
Other things to remember

A fuel system problem, such as a dirty carburettor or injector, can also cause poor mileage. Measure mileage over several full tanks, not one, and fill up the same way each time, so the number means something.

If nothing obvious explains it, have a mechanic look.

Fuel quality and the way the pump fills your tank can also change the numbers slightly, so use one or two trusted pumps and fill the same way each time.
Find the cause at home
Our certified mechanics check these items at your doorstep in Bengaluru. You get an itemised quote on WhatsApp first and approve it before work starts. See the service packages and prices.
faq: Why has my bike mileage suddenly dropped?

Common causes are low tyre pressure, a dry or loose chain, a dirty air filter, a worn spark plug, old oil, dragging brakes or changed riding conditions. A mechanic can check these quickly and fix what is found.
How can I measure my bike's mileage properly?

Fill the tank fully, reset the trip meter, ride as usual, then fill up again the same way and divide distance by litres added. Repeat over a few tanks for a reliable figure. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Does tyre pressure affect mileage?

Yes. Under-inflated tyres have more rolling resistance, so the engine uses more fuel. They also wear faster and handle worse. Check pressure regularly using your owner's manual figures, and do it when tyres are cold.

title: Tyre Pressure and Tyre Wear Guide | Mechanix Pro
desc: Correct tyre pressure and a regular wear check keep your bike safer and tyres lasting longer. Learn how to check both and read uneven wear.
h1: Tyre pressure and tyre wear: what to check
lead: Tyres are the only part of your bike touching the road. Pressure and wear checks take a couple of minutes and matter a lot.
sections: Getting pressure right

The correct pressure is in your owner's manual or on a sticker on the bike. It often differs for front and rear, and for riding with a pillion. Check it when the tyres are cold, because heat from riding raises the reading.

Check at least every couple of weeks, and before a long ride.

Keep a small, reliable gauge on your bike or at home. Pump gauges at petrol stations are not always accurate.
What wrong pressure does

Too low and the tyre heats up, wears the edges, feels heavy to steer and uses more fuel. Too high and the contact patch shrinks, grip drops and the ride gets harsh.

Both make the tyre wear out faster.

A tyre can lose pressure slowly without a visible puncture, so a tyre that looks fine can still be well below the right pressure.
Checking tread and condition

Most tyres have wear indicator marks in the tread grooves. When the tread reaches them, the tyre is due for replacement. Look for cracks in the rubber, bulges, cuts and objects stuck in the tread.

Old tyres can harden and crack even if the tread looks fine.
Reading uneven wear

Wear down the centre often means over-inflation. Wear on both edges suggests under-inflation. Wear on one side or in patches can point to alignment, suspension or brake problems.

Those need a proper check, not just a new tyre.

A tyre that wears faster on one side than the other, or wears in patches, is a hint for a mechanic to check alignment and suspension.
Tyre age and storage

Rubber ages with time, sun and heat, even without use. Small cracks in the sidewall or tread grooves, and a hard, shiny surface, are signs of an old tyre.

The tyre sidewall carries a code that shows when it was made. Ask your mechanic to read it for you, and consider replacing very old tyres even if the tread looks good.

title: Bike Breakdown on the Road: What to Do First | Mechanix Pro
desc: If your bike breaks down in Bengaluru, safety comes first. A calm step-by-step guide: get off the road, make yourself seen and call for roadside help.
h1: What to do when your bike breaks down on the road
lead: A breakdown is stressful, but a few calm steps keep you safe. Do these in order and do not rush into a roadside repair.
sections: Get out of traffic first

As soon as the bike falters, signal and move to the side, away from moving vehicles. Choose a spot with a clear view, and avoid blind bends, flyovers and the middle of a junction.

If you cannot ride it, push it to a safer place.

If you are on a highway or an elevated road, move as far from the traffic lane as you can, and never stand between the bike and moving traffic.
Make yourself visible

Switch on the hazard lights if your bike has them. At night, stay where headlights can see you, and stand away from the road, not beside the bike in the traffic lane. A reflective jacket or a torch helps.

Keep your phone charged and your location easy to describe.

Share your live location with a friend or family member, along with a short note about what happened. It helps someone know where you are while you wait.
Simple checks only if it is safe

Check the obvious: fuel, kill switch, side stand, a loose battery wire or a flat tyre. Do not open hot parts, and do not keep cranking the engine, which can drain the battery or flood the engine.

Do not attempt anything that needs tools in traffic.
Do not push your luck

If the bike smells of fuel, smokes, overheats or makes a harsh noise, switch off and stay clear. Riding a damaged bike can turn a small repair into a big one, and can be unsafe for you.

If the brakes or steering feel wrong, do not ride on.

A bike that has been in a fall should be checked for bent levers, leaking fluids and loose parts before it is ridden again, even if it seems to run.
Be ready before it happens

Keep your documents, a basic tool kit and a charged phone with you. Save the number of roadside help and a trusted contact. A power bank is a small thing that can matter a lot.

Regular servicing is the best way to prevent breakdowns. Most roadside problems start as small signs, like a hard start, a weak battery or a worn tyre, that were easy to miss.

title: Fuel Quality and Carburettor Cleaning | Mechanix Pro
desc: Poor fuel and clogged jets cause rough running and low mileage. Learn the basics of fuel quality and when carburettor or injector cleaning helps.
h1: Fuel quality and carburettor or injector cleaning basics
lead: The fuel system is easy to ignore until the bike starts coughing. Here is what affects it and what a cleaning actually does.
sections: Why fuel quality matters

Dirt, water or stale fuel can clog tiny passages in the fuel system. A bike that sits unused for weeks can end up with varnish from old petrol, which blocks jets and injectors.

Use fuel from busy, trusted pumps, and avoid running the tank right down to the bottom, where sediment collects.

Fuel filters and strainers also collect dirt, and a blocked one starves the engine. Many bikes have one in the tank or the fuel line.
Carburettor or injector?

Older and some budget bikes use a carburettor, which mixes air and fuel through small jets. Newer bikes use fuel injection, where an injector sprays fuel and a computer decides how much.

Your manual or a mechanic can tell you which your bike has.

If your bike is a few years old and has covered a lot of city distance, deposits can build up even with decent fuel.
Signs of a dirty fuel system

• Hard starting or stalling
  • Hesitation or jerking when you accelerate
  • A rough idle
  • Poor mileage
  • Black smoke or a strong fuel smell

These can also come from air filter, plug or electrical faults, so a proper diagnosis helps.
What cleaning involves

On a carburettor, the mechanic removes it, cleans the jets and passages and resets the idle and mixture. On an injected bike, cleaning may involve the throttle body and injectors, sometimes with a cleaning treatment.

A fuel additive can help in mild cases, but it will not fix a badly blocked jet.

Cleaning is not always the answer. If the jets or injectors are damaged, they need to be replaced, and a mechanic can tell the difference.
Habits that keep the system clean

Avoid letting the bike sit for months with fuel in it. If you will not ride for a long time, ask a mechanic what to do about the tank and the fuel lines.

Keep the tank cap sealed properly, and avoid filling from unknown roadside sources. Water can get in through a poorly sealed cap, especially during the monsoon.

See the service packages and prices and message us.
faq: Does carburettor cleaning improve mileage?

It can, if dirty jets were making the engine run poorly. Cleaning restores the correct air and fuel mix and smooths idle and pickup. If the poor mileage has other causes, such as a worn plug or air filter, cleaning alone will not fix it.
How do I know if my bike has bad petrol?

Signs include sudden rough running, stalling or hesitation soon after refuelling. If this starts right after a fill-up, tell your mechanic. The fuel tank and lines may need to be drained and cleaned. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Do fuel injectors need cleaning?

Injectors can get dirty over time, causing rough idle, hesitation and poor mileage. A mechanic can clean the throttle body and injectors if needed. Follow your owner's manual for the maintenance schedule on your model.

title: Headlight and Indicator Checks at Night | Mechanix Pro
desc: Night riding needs working lights. A simple pre-ride check of headlight, brake light, indicators and horn, plus signs the electrics need a mechanic.
h1: Headlight and indicator checks for night riding
lead: Lights help you see, and just as importantly, help others see you. A two-minute walk-around catches most problems.
sections: The five-minute check

• Headlight on low beam and high beam
  • Tail light and number plate light
  • Brake light, using both the lever and the pedal
  • All four indicators, front and rear
  • Horn

Do this at least weekly, and always before a night or long ride.

Ask a friend to stand behind the bike while you press the brake, so you can be sure the brake light works with both controls.
Dim or flickering lights

A headlight that has gone dim can mean an ageing bulb, a weak battery or a poor ground connection. Flickering often points to loose wiring or a failing regulator, which also affects charging.

If lights dim when you slow down, have the charging system tested.

Corroded bulb sockets and loose ground wires are among the most common hidden causes of electrical trouble, and they are cheap to fix when found.
Aim and cleanliness

A headlight that points too high dazzles other riders, and one that points too low reduces your view. Wipe the lens, because dirt and fogging cut the light. Check that the lens is not cracked, since water can get in.

Fitting very bright aftermarket bulbs without the right wiring can overload the circuit.
Indicators and flasher

If an indicator blinks fast, one bulb is probably out. If none works, check the flasher relay and fuse. Make sure you can see the indicators in daylight too.

Do not ride without working brake lights.

Turn signals that do not cancel by themselves, or that blink erratically, can point to a loose connector or a worn switch.
Riding smart at night

Slow down more than you would in the day, because potholes, speed breakers and animals are harder to see. Keep a good distance from the vehicle ahead and avoid looking straight into oncoming headlights.

Wear reflective gear and keep your helmet visor clean and scratch-free. A dirty or scratched visor makes glare much worse.

faq: Why is my bike headlight dim?

Common causes are an old bulb, a weak battery, loose or corroded connections or a charging fault. If the light dims at low revs and brightens when you accelerate, have the battery and charging system tested.
Why does my indicator blink fast?
A fast blink usually means a bulb on that side has failed or has the wrong rating. Replace the bulb with the correct one. If it persists, the flasher relay or wiring may need checking.

A quick check weekly is a good habit, and always before night rides or long trips. Check headlight, tail light, brake light, indicators and horn. Fix any failure straight away. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

title: How to Wash a Bike Without Damaging It | Mechanix Pro
desc: A bad wash can push water into bearings and electrics. A simple, safe method for washing your bike or scooter at home, and what to avoid.
h1: How to wash a bike without damaging it
lead: Washing keeps rust and grime away, but how you do it matters. Done wrong, it can push water where it should never go.
sections: Before you start

Let the engine and exhaust cool. Washing a hot bike can leave spots and, with a hot exhaust or discs, is not ideal. Park in the shade if you can.

Cover the exhaust outlet and air intake if you are unsure, and make sure the fuel cap is closed.

A bucket, a sponge, a soft cloth and a mild shampoo are enough. You do not need expensive products for a good wash.
Use gentle water

Rinse with a low-pressure stream. High-pressure jets can push water into wheel bearings, the chain seals, the switch gear, the instrument cluster and the air box. Keep spray away from these.

Do the same on electric scooters, and keep water away from the charging port.

Rinse the engine area only with a gentle stream. Do not spray water directly into the exhaust or the air intake.
Soap, sponge and cloth

Use a mild bike or car shampoo and a soft sponge or microfibre cloth. Wash from top to bottom, and rinse often. Avoid harsh detergents, which can dull paint and dry out rubber and plastics.

Use a separate brush for wheels and the chain, so grit does not scratch the paint.
Dry and protect

Dry with a clean cloth, especially around the chain, bolts and the underside, where water collects. Then lubricate the chain, and check that the brakes work normally. Press the brake lightly a few times to dry the pads.

Avoid putting polish or silicone shine on the seat, tyres or brake parts, because it makes them slippery.

Do not use degreaser on rubber seals or plastic parts, and keep any chain cleaner away from the tyres and brakes.
How often to wash

Wash when the bike is visibly dirty, after a muddy or rainy ride and after riding near salt or dust. Dirt that sits on paint and metal holds moisture and speeds up rust.

Do not wash it every day if you do not need to. Frequent washing can wear off lubricants and thin out wax. A quick wipe with a damp cloth is enough on most days.
When a wash shows a problem

Washing is a good time to spot oil leaks, loose parts, cracked rubber or a rusty chain. If you find something, Mechanix Pro's certified mechanics can check it at your doorstep in Bengaluru.

See the service packages and prices and message us for a quote on WhatsApp.
faq: Can I use a pressure washer on my bike?
It is best to avoid high pressure, which can force water into bearings, electrics and the air box. Use a gentle stream, keep spray away from sensitive parts, and dry the bike and chain afterwards.
Should I wash my bike when the engine is hot?
No. Let the engine and exhaust cool first. Hot parts can cause water spots, and cold water on hot metal is not good for it. Park in the shade and wash once everything is cool.
What should I do after washing my bike?
Dry it with a clean cloth, lubricate the chain, and press the brake lightly a few times to dry the pads. Check that lights and controls work normally, and avoid slippery polish on seats and tyres.

title: Storing Your Bike While You Travel | Mechanix Pro
desc: Leaving a bike unused for weeks can flatten the battery and age the fuel. How to store a bike or scooter before a trip, and what to check when you return.
h1: How to store your bike when you travel
lead: A bike left alone for weeks can come back with a dead battery and stale fuel. A little preparation before you leave avoids that.
sections: Clean and park it right

Wash and dry the bike, and lubricate the chain. Park it somewhere dry, covered and safe. A breathable cover is better than plastic, which traps moisture and can cause rust.

Use the centre stand or a paddock stand if you have one, so the tyres do not develop flat spots.

A bike stored outdoors needs a cover and a firm, level spot. Check that the cover is tied down so wind does not rub it against the paint.
Fuel and battery

Fuel can go stale over time, so a nearly empty or very full tank each has trade-offs. Follow your manual, and for long storage, ask a mechanic about fuel stabiliser. For a short trip, keep a reasonable amount in the tank.

A battery slowly discharges when parked. For long absences, a trickle charger designed for your battery type helps, or disconnect it as your manual advises.

If someone can start the bike and let it run for a short time every week or two, that helps the battery and the fuel system. Ask your mechanic what suits your bike.
Tyres and brakes

Inflate the tyres to the correct pressure, or slightly higher if your manual allows, since they lose air over time. Do not leave the parking brake or the rear brake pressed for long periods.

Avoid leaving the bike where it can be hit or knocked over.
When you return

Check tyre pressure, fuel, battery, oil level and brakes before you ride. Start the bike and let it idle for a moment. Ride gently at first, and listen for new noises.

If it will not start, do not keep cranking. Get it checked.

After a long break, check the brake fluid and the chain, and look under the bike for fresh drips or leaks.
Safety and security while away

Lock the steering, use a disc lock or a chain if you have one, and park in a well-lit, secure place. Tell someone you trust that the bike will be unused, so they can keep an eye on it.

Take a few photos of the bike before you leave, and keep your documents with you. It makes things simpler if there is any problem while you are away.

faq: How do I store my bike for a few weeks?

Clean it, lubricate the chain, park it covered and dry, keep tyres inflated, and look after the battery with a suitable charger or as your manual advises. Check everything before you ride again. Ask for an itemised quote on WhatsApp before any work starts.
Should I leave fuel in the tank when I store my bike?
For short breaks, a sensible amount is fine. For long storage, fuel can go stale, so ask a mechanic about stabiliser or follow your owner's manual. Always check for fuel smell or leaks before riding.
Why will my bike not start after sitting for weeks?

The battery may have discharged, the fuel may have gone stale, or the carburettor jets may be clogged. Avoid cranking repeatedly. A mechanic can charge or test the battery and check the fuel system. Your owner's manual has the exact guidance for your model.

desc: The first service is important for a new bike or scooter. Why it matters, what it usually covers, when it is due and how it relates to your warranty.
h1: First service of a new bike: what to know
lead: A new bike needs its first service sooner than you might think. It is a small step that protects the engine and your warranty.
sections: Why the first service matters

During the first period of use, moving parts settle in, and tiny metal particles can end up in the oil. The first service replaces that oil and checks that everything has bedded in properly.

It also catches loose bolts, cable stretch and small adjustments early.

Some riders feel the bike is too new to need a service, but it is the best moment to catch small things while it is still fresh.
When it is due

Your owner's manual and service booklet give the timing, usually after a short distance or a short time from purchase, whichever comes first. Many makers want it done on time to keep the warranty valid.

Do not skip it or push it far past the due point.

Keep a note of your purchase date and the odometer reading on delivery, so you can see exactly when the first service is due.
What it usually covers

Typically an oil change, and an oil filter where fitted, along with chain adjustment and lubrication, brake and clutch checks, cable adjustments, a tightening check of key bolts, tyre pressure and a battery and lights check.

Exact items depend on the model, so follow the booklet.
Warranty questions

Warranty terms differ between makers. Some require servicing at authorised centres for certain claims, while others have different conditions. Read your warranty booklet, or ask the dealer, before choosing where to get it done.

Keep your service records and bills.

Ask the service centre or mechanic to stamp or sign the service booklet, and keep a copy of the bill, because both help when you sell the bike later.
Running in your new bike

Many makers advise riding gently during the early period: avoid very high speeds, very low gears at low revs and sudden hard acceleration. Your manual gives the exact guidance for your model.

Vary your speed, avoid long idling and let the engine warm up gently. This helps the parts bed in evenly and sets a good base for the life of the bike.

title: Second-Hand Bike Inspection Checklist | Mechanix Pro
desc: Buying a used bike or scooter? A practical checklist covering papers, engine, brakes, tyres, frame and a test ride, and why a mechanic's opinion helps.
h1: Second-hand bike inspection checklist
lead: A used bike can be great value, but only if you know what you are buying. Take this checklist along, and if possible, take a mechanic too.
sections: Check the papers first

Look at the registration certificate, insurance, service records and any pending dues. Make sure the registration number, engine number and chassis number on the bike match the documents. If they do not, walk away.

Ask who the registered owner is and whether the transfer will be done properly.

Check whether the bike has any loan or hypothecation entry on the papers, and ask for proof that it has been cleared if so.
Look at the body and frame

Walk around the bike in good light. Look for fresh paint on one part only, bent handlebars or fork tubes, a twisted frame, cracked plastics and uneven panel gaps, which can suggest a past accident. Check for rust, especially on the exhaust and underneath.

Sit on it and check that it stands straight.

Look under the bike and around the engine for oil or fluid stains. A very clean engine on an old bike can mean a leak was washed away just before the sale.
Engine, brakes and tyres

Cold-start the engine and listen for rattles or knocking. Check for smoke, oil leaks and uneven idle. Test brakes, clutch and gears. Look at tyre wear and age, the chain and sprockets, and the battery.

Brakes and tyres are safety items, so budget for replacing them if they are worn.
Take a test ride

Ride at a few speeds. The bike should track straight, brake without pulling and change gears smoothly. Listen for knocks from the suspension over bumps, and check that all lights, indicators, horn and instruments work.

Do not rush. A seller who hurries you is a warning sign.

Ride it on a bumpy stretch as well as a smooth one. Some faults only show up when the suspension and frame are working hard.
Costs to keep in mind

A used bike often needs a service soon after purchase, and may need tyres, a chain set, brake pads or a battery. Factor these in when you decide what to pay.

Ask for the service history if there is one. Regular records from a known workshop are a good sign, and a seller who cannot say when it was last serviced is a signal to be careful.

faq: What should I check when buying a used bike?

Check the papers and that engine and chassis numbers match, then inspect the body and frame for accident signs, test the engine, brakes, tyres and lights, and take a test ride. Get a mechanic to inspect it too.
How can I tell if a used bike has been in an accident?

Look for fresh paint on only one part, bent handlebars or forks, a twisted frame, cracked plastics and uneven panel gaps. A mechanic can check alignment and hidden damage more reliably than a quick look.
Is it worth getting a mechanic to inspect a second-hand bike?
Yes. A mechanic can spot worn parts, hidden repairs and engine problems you may miss, and can tell you what servicing it will need. It can save you from an expensive surprise after you pay.

lead: If you landed here looking for car service, here is a straight answer about what we do and where to go instead.
sections: What Mechanix Pro does

Mechanix Pro focuses on two-wheelers: doorstep bike and scooter service by certified mechanics, plus roadside help, across Bengaluru. That is where our training, tools and experience are.

We would rather say this honestly than take on a car we are not set up for.

Our team knows two-wheelers well, and that is the area where we can promise quality work, so we keep our focus there.
Who handles cars

Cars are handled by our partner Axlio, which is a separate business. For car service and car repairs, visit the Axlio partner page and follow the steps there.

Axlio also handles spare parts, so that page is useful if you are looking for parts too.

If you are not sure whether we can help with a vehicle, send us a short message on WhatsApp and we will tell you honestly.
Choosing a car service in general

Whoever you choose, a few habits help. Ask for an itemised quote before work starts. Ask which parts will be used. Ask what warranty applies and what it covers. Keep your bills and service records.

For safety items such as brakes and tyres, ask the mechanic to explain what is worn and why.
Two-wheeler in the family too

Many households in Bengaluru have both a car and a bike or scooter. If you have a two-wheeler, our certified mechanics come to your home or office, and you get an itemised quote on WhatsApp first.

You pay only after you approve it, and our work carries a 30-day service warranty.

Whatever you drive, regular service is the cheapest way to avoid a breakdown, and a written quote is the best protection against surprises.
If you ride a bike or scooter too

Two-wheelers have their own needs, such as chain care, clutch and CVT checks and tyre wear. Regular care helps them last longer and ride more safely in city traffic.

If you are not sure when your bike last had a proper service, a quick check is a good place to begin. We can look at the basics and tell you what really needs doing.
Get started
For your bike or scooter, see the service packages and prices and message us on WhatsApp for a quote. For your car, begin with the Axlio page.

Our partner Axlio handles cars. It is a separate business from Mechanix Pro. You can reach it through the partner page on our website, which explains how to book car service or spare parts. A mechanic can check this properly at your doorstep.
Can Mechanix Pro help with my bike if I also have a car?

Yes. Our certified mechanics service bikes and scooters at your home or office in Bengaluru. You get an itemised quote on WhatsApp first and pay only after you approve it, with a 30-day warranty on the work.
